items.name: Readability
items.evidence: The names are clear (worker, factory, errors, pending), and the docstring explains the ordering, error and cancellation behaviour. The cancel-and-wait loop has a comment. `it`, `e` and `w` are short but used in idiomatic iterator, except and loop spots.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: It is one roughly 50-line function. It rebuilds structured concurrency by hand (create_task + gather + a manual `while pending: ... asyncio.wait` cancel loop) instead of using asyncio.TaskGroup plus a Semaphore, which makes the logic longer and harder to change.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: It validates `max_concurrent < 1`, waits for cleanup even through repeated cancellation, and retrieves worker exceptions. But `errors.append(e)` followed by `raise errors[0]` silently drops every error after the first, with no ExceptionGroup.

items.name: Failures and degenerate arguments
items.evidence: Empty lists and invalid limits are handled (`raise ValueError`). But when a task fails, the code does not cancel the other running tasks. It keeps starting queued tasks and raises only the first error at the end, so later failures are lost. It does not hang or leak tasks.

items.name: Required signature and import behaviour
items.name_zh: 签名与导入行为符合要求
items.evidence: `async def run_tasks(tasks: list[Callable[[], Awaitable[None]]], max_concurrent: int) -> None`. Workers call `factory()` lazily, only when a slot is free. It uses only the standard library and has no side effects at import.
